item.title: Why didn't Nvidia have a succession plan?
item.description:
Until this week, Nvidia only ever had one CEO: Jensen Huang. Now, Colette Kress — previously the company’s CFO — will take on the role while the company searches for a permanent replacement. It’s the job of a corporate board to cultivate a successor, but that didn’t happen at Nvidia. This morning, we unpack what went wrong. item.title: Bucking the national trend, S.D. Democrats continue to flounder
item.description:
While Democrats swept the Midterm elections nationally, with a "tsunami" that reached Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and possibly Mississippi, in South Dakota the Republicans scored yet another sweep, winning all the statewide races by somewhere between 58% (Heather Baxter for Secretary of State) and 64% (Marty Jackley for Congress) of the total vote.

South Dakota Democrats did gain legislative seats, moving from just 8 out of 105 legislators all the way up to 12 out of 105 legislators, but these gains were entirely in the Sioux Falls area. Even the districts representing our nine Native American reservations, which were designed for Democratic wins, were swept by Republican candidates, with the lone exception of Eric Emery, who will continue to represent the Rosebud reservation. 

Why did South Dakota buck the national trend and go solidly Republican at a time when Donald Trump inspired so many Democratic victories? Have South Dakota Democrats been down so long that we can no longer pick ourselves up?

It's a fact that no South Dakota Democrat has won a statewide race since 2008, when Sen. Tim Johnson and Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin both won landslide re-elections. That was also the year that Barack Obama won the Presidency, earning almost 45% of the vote in South Dakota and carrying 14 of our 66 counties, including Minnehaha and Brown. 

In the years that followed, rural America turned sharply away from Obama and the Democrats and helped elect Donald Trump at the end of Obama's Presidency. As America has become totally polarized between the major urban areas, which are increasingly Democratic, and the small cities and rural areas which are heavily Republican, South Dakota has clearly identified as a red state. While Kansas just elected its first Democratic Senator since 1932, South Dakota has not elected a Democratic Governor since 1974.

We used to pride ourselves on having some of the highest voter turnouts in America. This month, only 49% of South Dakota voters bothered to go to the polls. As many voters perceived that none of our major races were actually competitive, the low turnout became a self-fulfilling prophecy. One party dominance is not good for democracy. 

As we move toward 2028, when America will elect a new President, what can we do to start to rebuild a genuine two-party system in South Dakota? This state was very competitive politically from the late 1950's into the early 2000's.

Many of our rural communities actually leaned Democratic in those years. George McGovern single-handedly built a strong, competitive Democratic Party, which elected Jim Abourezk, Dick Kneip, Tom Daschle, Tim Johnson and McGovern himself. As the Trump Presidency continues to flounder, South Dakota Democrats need to return to serious grassroots organizing.

This needs to expand beyond the Sioux Falls metro area to our small cities, small towns and rural areas. South Dakotans need to be convinced that their votes really might make a difference. Then we may be able to get out of our one-party rut.

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

item.title: Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up
item.description:
A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

item.title: What are the new rules for parenting in the digital age?
item.description:
An increasing number of school districts are restricting phones in the classroom, and a series of major lawsuits against social media companies have led some platforms to make significant changes to how they operate. But, bans or not, the reality is that kids are going to encounter this stuff at some point.


Pamela Wisniewski, at the International Computer Science Institute, says kids need guidance to learn how to use technology responsibly.


More on this

ChatGPT for Teens' safeguards don't work, risk assessment finds — from Marketplace

item.title: New Democratic congress should be progressive, not retributive
item.description:
The November 3 election gave the Democratic Party in Congress a strong majority in both houses. As a result, they have the ability to pass anything they want. That majority came about because large numbers of independents and moderate republicans were upset and disappointed in the actions of president Trump. The war, the economy, the deficits and the excesses of ICE were major factors in the defection resulting in those “swing” voters voting for democrats in the election. They voted against those items and simply want them to end and expect Democrats to do that.

Many or most democrats voted because they are angry at the vicious and vindictive way Trump has attacked liberals, immigrants and institutions. In addition to the “swing” items, many or most democrats voted for revenge. They want Congress to be as vindictive in return as Trump was to them.

The democratic response in Congress can be negative or positive. If they choose to respond negatively and to cater to the democratic base and be vindictive, they can impeach, investigate and attack this administration, and there is more than enough reason to do so. 

However, impeaching Trump for the umpteenth time accomplishes nothing. There aren’t votes to convict and remove him from office and worse yet, impeachment could generate sympathy for Trump among the moderates that voted against him.He will not be on the ballot in 2028 and those moderates need a new reason to continue to vote democratic.

Even if they could get the Republican votes to remove him, it would allow JD Vance to have the advantage of incumbency in the next election. They can spend lots of time investigating the myriad of questionable and legally dubious actions of this administration. 

But that is not what the swing voters voted for. They want it to discontinue in the future, but the past is past and they only want a better future. A negative Democratic congress risks losing their gains among swing voters. In the short term it would feel good, but the long term loss of those voters would be costly.

A positive response would be to enact legislation that is popular among the majority of Americans rather than attacks that only appeal to the base. There are many positive bills that the congress could pass in the next budget that would be popular among both democrats and swing voters. Among them:

Deficit reduction. Clinton left a budget that did not require borrowing. The congress could reverse the Bush and Trump tax cuts and return to the balanced budget tax rates of Clinton. And a spending plan within those limits. Increase taxes on billionaires. In addition to the Clinton tax rates, a modest increase in tax rates on the highest income levels would be popular and help balance the budget.

Reducing or eliminating tax subsidies to corporations. Not necessary to raise tax rates, but subsidies such as oil companies that made three times as much profit during the war as they did the year previously.

Defunding ICE. Make major reductions in ICE while requiring professional behavior. The training and leadership has been abysmal and Congress should require improvements.

Defunding the war. Trump has ramped up the military to be an offensive weapon of war on other countries, rather than a defense of America first. The military needed to defend America is vastly smaller that one that wages war. We don’t need more veterans of FOREIGN wars.

Restoring fairness to all Americans. Restore the university research that has maintained American technological and intellectual leadership in the world and been the solid base for economic growth.

Limit the ability to levy tariffs which are a sales tax on Americans. Tariffs were the single largest tax increase in history. Some tariffs are necessary or at least useful.

Restore military aid to Ukraine, allowing them to resist tyranny.

These initiatives do two things that are advantageous to Democrats. They show that the Democratic Party can not only complain, but can govern. That is critical. They also put Donald Trump in an impossible position. These items are popular, but Trump would not want Democrats to be able to take credit for them. However, vetoing them would continue to alienate swing voters. Worse yet, vetoing a budget would shut down the country.

Trump has had four government shutdowns and none have been beneficial to him. The 2018 shutdown was particularly humiliating. He can’t afford that. It is the positive way to generate negative results for Trump and pave the way for future victories.

The Democratic Congress will have to demonstrate a certain amount of vindictiveness to placate the democratic base. And there should be consequences for the outrageous acts of this administration.

But it should not be the focus. Those investigations should not be where Democrats spend their media attention. The media will cover it extensively because it is news. The Democratic congress should focus its attention on showing America the positive things they believe in and are working on, not just because it is good for America, but because promoting positive bills will demonstrate the ability to govern and can maintain the coalition that they will need in future elections.

John Cunningham of Sioux Falls has spent his career in local government finance, including in Fulton County, Ga., and Atlanta. He has a master of public administration from Harvard and has done consultant work in four foreign countries

item.title: What's in a jobless claim?
item.description:
First-time jobless claims — that’s the number of people who filed for unemployment in a given week — are at a 57-year low. Sounds good, right? Sure, except changes to the unemployment insurance system have narrowed the pool of eligible recipients. And it doesn’t include the rising long-term unemployment rate. So the question is, are jobless claims a reliable economic indicator anymore? Also in this episode: War in the Middle East gives U.S. LNG producers a leg up, the Nashville Symphony recieves critical support from an unlikely source, and AI investors have their eyes glued to CoreWeave earnings.

item.title: QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm
item.description:
QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company says the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.

item.title: Reddit pivots to a login-only experience
item.description:
Reddit announced it will soon require users to log in to see much of the helpful human-generated content on its site. Why? Because traffic, and thus advertising, has taken a hit since AI started summarizing its data.


It's the latest development to threaten the old model of the open internet, says Sarah Gilbert, who researches online communities at the Citizens and Technology Lab at Cornell and is also active in r/askhistorians. She says the new login requirement puts up a wall between humans on the internet and is likely to discourage future contributions to the site.


More on this:


“Reddit moves to logged-in experience as AI eats search” from Axios


“AI Is Killing Wikipedia’s Human Traffic” from Gizmodo

item.title: ‘Hell sucks.’ A veteran reflects on life and death at the DMZ, 1967
item.description:
Author’s note: This year is the 60th anniversary of my deployment to South Vietnam, a milestone I commemorate by rerunning this piece, which I posted a couple of years ago – John Tsitrian

It’s Veterans Day and I’m revisiting the Nam.

In the above pic, I had just come back to the relatively secure airstrip at Dong Ha, slightly south of the Demilitarized Zone, after spending a few weeks at some — pick an adjective, they all fit — desolate, remote, bleak, lonely, dark, depressing, forlorn, gloomy, wretched and neglected outpost along the nearby Cua Viet river, where rocket and artillery attacks were part of the daily routine and potshots into our perimeter were an occasional part of the nightly routine.

It sucked, and it wasn’t just about me. Describing life for all the Marines along the DMZ, Dispatches author Michael Herr titled his piece about us “Hell Sucks.”

That pretty well summed it up.

It was at the DMZ that I had my first encounter with incomprehensibility and surrealism, where waste of materials and humans was supposed to be an acceptable consequence of an American crusade to fight off, in then President Lyndon Johnson’s words, “the deepening shadow of Communist China,” which was a principal source of supplies and weapons to our enemy, North Vietnam. Together, the Chinese and the North Vietnamese were characterized by American cold warriors as “the yellow peril.”

Johnson sold the war to the American public with that kind of rhetoric, but it turned out to be baloney.

How’s that? Well, in 1972 with the war still raging, LBJ’s successor Richard Nixon set out to make friends with China, even though Chinese weaponry was still targeting and killing American troops. Despite that, Nixon was proudly and optimistically visiting Beijing. He was busy opening up trade and diplomatic channels with the country that LBJ just a few years earlier described as a fearsome spectre and “deepening shadow.”

Confused? I was.

Was China LBJ’s threat to the free world, or was it Nixon’s friend and potential diplomatic and trading partner? The war was so messed up that the two presidents of the era couldn’t get their stories straight.

To me, it’s little wonder that so many Vietnam vets have had post-war mental health issues. The confused situation of our war was indeed surreal, if not altogether schizophrenic. A 2022 Veterans Administration study on the subject concluded that “veterans who served in Vietnam, Cambodia, or Laos during the Vietnam War have a higher prevalence of mental health issues, particularly PTSD, compared with both other Vietnam-era Veterans and non-Veterans.”

The whole mangled mess of it was an exercise in muddled objectives and wasted resources, so much so that when people died we didn’t say that they were killed. We said that they “got wasted.” 

Now, nearly sixty years later, I’m a generally appreciated veteran. I couldn’t be more pleased. I like my status, but must note that thanks to that war, I also couldn’t be more skeptical about the utterances of our political leadership. That coarsened attitude has pushed me to speak out via my earlier stints as a feature writer and newspaper columnist and now as the publisher and editor of this blog.  

With my fellow vets on this Veterans Day, I thank you for your attention and appreciation – as well as your support and patience when it comes to encountering veterans who were permanently scarred by experiences like mine.  

I also hope that as you acknowledge and honor our veterans, you do so with a commitment to exercise some critical thought when listening to the rhetoric of our political class. That would be a nice outcome when you think of what veterans sacrificed in pursuit of their service to our country.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

Photo: Dong Ha, Vietnam, 1967, taken by a buddy

item.title: House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
item.description: The House has turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The vote Tuesday halted an effort to remove Hegseth as Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran. The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary. They rejected the impeachment effort led by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.

item.title: Inflation just won't quit
item.description:
Inflation is still running hot, according to the latest CPI report on consumer prices. In October, costs were up 0.4% from the previous month, 0.3% without food or energy. Economists say its a sign those high gas prices have permeated this economy, indirectly raising the cost of just about everything else. The good news? Crude oil, gas, and diesel prices are actually starting to fall. We’ll break down why. Plus: Retailers try to block AI shopping agents and some Americans avoid spending their retirement savings.

item.title: Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders
item.description:
Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

item.title: Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years
item.description:
Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

item.title: A data center moves next door. Do you stay or go?
item.description:
Many communities across the country voted last week to ban or limit data center development. Elsewhere, people have to rely on local elected officials to make data center decisions for them, and in many places — like Bessemer, Alabama — they’re not happy with those decisions. There, a mayor’s been ousted, a swath of local forest has been cleared, and dozens of people are debating whether to move. Also on the show: hotter-than-expected inflation and a look at debts in collections.

item.title: Why it matters who owns U.S. debt
item.description:
Back in the early 2000s, foreign investors owned the majority of the debt issued by the U.S. government. Since then, the market for U.S. debt has shifted toward domestic investors. Now, foreign investors own just a quarter of all U.S. debt. That shift can have consequences for interest rates during periods of turmoil. We dig in. Also, communities across the country have been banding together to fight data center projects, but many local governments approve them anyway.

item.title: Can communities and data centers find common ground?
item.description:
The message that Americans have no love for AI data centers rang out loud and clear in the midterms, with dozens of jurisdictions voting to stop their construction and electing governors who oppose them.


Where they are still allowed, it's likely we'll see some concessions from data center developers — like community benefit agreements. These agreements have been used for decades for big building projects like transit or sports arenas.


Late last year, the city of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, signed one of the first major CBAs with data center developers.


Devashree Saha, director of the U.S. Clean Energy Economy Program at the World Resources Institute, explains how the agreement came together and where it might fall short.


More on this


After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming — from Tech Crunch


OpenAI pledges no NDAs, protection from power costs in data center deals — from Seeking Alpha


Powering Progress: How Community Benefits Agreements Can Drive Responsible Data Center Development — from the World Resources Institute
item.source:markdown:
The message that Americans have no love for AI data centers rang out loud and clear in the midterms, [with dozens of jurisdictions voting to stop their construction and electing governors who oppose them](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/data-center-rejected-voters-us-challenging-ai-boom-rcna607451).
Where they are still allowed, it's likely we'll see some concessions from data center developers — like community benefit agreements. These agreements have been used for decades for big building projects like transit or sports arenas.
Late last year, the city of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, signed [one of the first major CBAs with data center developers.](https://www.cityoflancasterpa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Community-Benefits-Agreement-Summary-1-1.pdf)
Devashree Saha, director of the U.S. Clean Energy Economy Program at the World Resources Institute, explains how the agreement came together and where it might fall short.
### More on this
[After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/04/after-the-midterms-a-bigger-clash-over-data-centers-could-be-coming/) — from Tech Crunch
[OpenAI pledges no NDAs, protection from power costs in data center deals](https://seekingalpha.com/news/4666317-openai-pledges-no-ndas-protection-from-power-costs-in-data-center-deals) — from Seeking Alpha
[Powering Progress: How Community Benefits Agreements Can Drive Responsible Data Center Development](https://www.wri.org/technical-perspectives/community-benefits-agreements-data-centers) — from the World Resources Institute

item.title: Last week's midterm elections were a requiem for MAGA
item.description:
I was road-tripping through Minnesota last weekend and couldn’t resist taking the pic above from my car. Sorry about the resolution, but the posting of a worn out Trump sign on a dilapidated building was too rich with symbolism to bypass.  

After several years of its mobilization and coalescence, after institutionalization by the Trump administration, and after one policy failure followed by another and then another, the MAGA  movement is exhausted … and expunged.

Trump loyalists trying to tout tariffs and the righteousness of our war with Iran just got their political rear ends handed to them, some in states like Kansas, Mississippi and Texas where Republicans just don’t lose.  

I’m as prone to gloat as the next guy and gladly broadcast my giddiness over the election results last Tuesday. It’s not so much that I’m pro-Democrat as it is that I’m anti-Trump.

From my perspective as a pre-Trump Republican, I’m hoping that my former party can see the light and understand the damage —no, carnage — that Trump has inflicted on the GOP.

The party has to cleanse itself of Trump’s ideological and political detritus. Examples?

  • On trade policy the GOP has to re-engage the principles of free trade that have been a cornerstone of conservatism since the 1950s and forward to the Reagan-Bush years

  • On immigration, Republicans have to go back to the days when they championed immigration.They understood that pro-immigration policies, including finding pathways to legalization for undocumented residents, were among the reasons that our economy prospered.

  • On alliances, Republicans have to go back to a time when they championed NATO, which Trump has said is “obsolete.” A unified front like NATO ensures that its members face threats side-by-side rather than in isolation.

  • Republicans need to redevelop a friendlier approach to our immediate neighbors Mexico and Canada. Why Trump feels he needs to pick a fight with Canada is beyond understanding.  

  • Embracing science again would be a nice reversion back to the days when Republicans “had a great deal of confidence” in the scientific community. Dragging their feet on climate change and putting the scientifically-challenged Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., in charge of Health and Human Services are, on the face of it, evidence that Trump’s party doesn’t give a damn about science.,

Trump and MAGA are worn out and used up. They’re helplessly ineffective and increasingly irrelevant. The problems they promised to solve are as burdensome as ever. It's time for some collective introspection by the GOP. It’s time to render Donald Trump politically useless and leave him to his self-glorifying dreams of building pretentious monuments and promoting his own silly brand.

There’s work to be done, Republicans. Time to get started

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.  

Photo: Minnesota roadside scene last weekend, John Tsitrian

item.title: The cost of executive blunders
item.description:
It’s a common trope in Big Tech: an iconic CEO, interchangable with the brand itself. Jobs and Apple, Zuckerberg and Meta, Altman and OpenAI. Nvidia is no exception — its leather jacket-clad CEO Jensen Huang has superstar status among Silicon Valley elites. So what happens when that image is shattered? In this episode, celebrity CEOs come with steep consequences for a business and its investors. Plus: Mortgage rates decline modestly in the wake of the midterms and young consumers give new meaning to “Made in China” labels.

item.description:

item.title: Tesla launches Robotaxi in San Antonio with a 274 sq mi geofence on paper
item.description:
Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.

But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.

item.title: October was warmest on record. Will Dems address climate change?
item.description:
This year’s October was the warmest on record. Maybe more sobering is the news that it was the third consecutive month to exceed the warming threshold set by the 2016 Paris Climate Agreement, which was ratified by 194 countries, including the United States. 

The U.S. pulled out of the agreement, first in 2017, then, after Biden rejoined the accord during his presidency, again in January 2025 because President Trump, after a decision that was widely supported by conservatives, said its allotment of timelines for compliance gave an economic advantage to China and other nations at the expense of the United States.

Others disagreed, but the decision stuck.

So where is the United States now on climate change? Not a very good place. 

The University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute concludes that “climate change is no longer a problem for the distant future. The effects of climate change are being seen and felt today.” You can scan the report for a detailed summation of the economic effects of climate change. A general conclusion is that warming temperatures will cost the U.S. anywhere from one to four percent of GDP by the end of the century.  

Of more specific relevance to a farm state like South Dakota, Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability says that “rising global temperatures will dampen the world’s capacity to produce food from most staple crops, even after accounting for economic development and adaptation by farmers.” 

Looking at this year’s situation, South Dakota’s farmers have been hit hard by drought, with producers in Brookings, Deuel, Hyde, and Stanley counties getting financial assistance from USDA because of severe or extended drought designations. The USDA statement reads “this disaster declaration highlights the continuing impact that drought can have on agricultural communities.”  

Note the words “continuing impact.”

Has the Trump administration done much about alleviating climate change?  No. In fact, his “drill, baby, drill” mantra is a direct assault on the whole notion that climate change is real and has to be addressed.

My hope is that the new congress, heavily weighted toward Democrats, will weigh in on climate change and bring some reality and substance into the U.S. approach toward it. 

And now that Trump has been so severely weakened, politically, by last week’s Democratic tsunami, let’s hope that our all-GOP representation can understand South Dakota’s stake in the future of climate change – and maybe stand up for their constituents who are dealing with it every day.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
This year’s October was the [warmest on record](https://abcnews.com/International/october-warmest-record-globally-el-nino-intensifies-report/story?id=137911248). Maybe more sobering is the news that it was the third consecutive month to exceed the warming threshold set by the [2016 Paris Climate Agreement](https://abcnews.com/International/paris-climate-agreement/story?id=43301507), which was ratified by 194 countries, including the United States.
The U.S. [pulled out of the agreement](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48504), first in 2017, then, after Biden rejoined the accord during his presidency, again in January 2025 because President Trump, after a decision that was [widely supported](https://www.heritage.org/environment/commentary/4-reasons-trump-was-right-pull-out-the-paris-agreement) by conservatives, said its allotment of timelines for compliance gave an economic advantage to China and other nations at the expense of the United States.
[Others disagreed](https://www.cfr.org/ten-best-ten-worst-us-foreign-policy-decisions/withdrawal-from-the-paris-climate-agreement/), but the decision stuck.
So where is the United States now on climate change? Not a very good place.
The [University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute](https://epic.uchicago.edu/area-of-focus/climate-change-and-the-us-economic-future/) concludes that _“climate change is no longer a problem for the distant future. The effects of climate change are being seen and felt today.”_ You can scan the report for a detailed summation of the economic effects of climate change. A general conclusion is that warming temperatures will cost the U.S. anywhere from one to four percent of GDP by the end of the century.
Of more specific relevance to a farm state like South Dakota, [Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability](https://sustainability.stanford.edu/news/climate-change-cuts-global-crop-yields-even-when-farmers-adapt/) says that _“rising global temperatures will dampen the world’s capacity to produce food from most staple crops, even after accounting for economic development and adaptation by farmers.”_
Looking at this year’s situation, South Dakota’s farmers have been [hit hard](https://southdakotaagconnection.com/news/south-dakota-farmers-gain-usda-drought-support) by drought, with producers in Brookings, Deuel, Hyde, and Stanley counties getting financial assistance from USDA because of severe or extended drought designations. The USDA statement reads _“this disaster declaration highlights the continuing impact that drought can have on agricultural communities.”_
Note the words _“continuing impact.”_
Has the Trump administration done much about alleviating climate change? [No](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/campaigns/2026/01/trump-impact-on-global-climate-action/). In fact, his [“drill, baby, drill” mantra](https://www.weforum.org/stories/energy-transition/us-enters-drill-era-top-energy-leader-oil-gas) is a direct assault on the whole notion that climate change is real and has to be addressed.
My hope is that the new congress, heavily weighted toward Democrats, will weigh in on climate change and bring some reality and substance into the U.S. approach toward it.
And now that Trump has been so severely weakened, politically, by last week’s Democratic tsunami, let’s hope that our all-GOP representation can understand South Dakota’s stake in the future of climate change – and maybe stand up for their constituents who are dealing with it every day.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles
item.description:
If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

item.title: Did voters disregard politics and feel they just couldn’t stand Trump ?
item.description:
Hee’s a quick take on the election.

It’s been interesting and sometimes comical watching people explaining the election results with excuses, analyses, rationalizations, anger, finger pointing, and hindsight.

Inflation, war with Iran, corruption, and ICE tactics have been cited as reasons why the Donald Trump presidency and the MAGA ideas were so soundly rejected.

Those things, large and small, were all part of it -  but perhaps there was also something else at play.

For those on the fence over the issues and the state of the nation, maybe one conspicuous thing could have been what pushed them over the edge:

Trump is just plain unlikable.

He is seen as cruel, vindictive, corrupt, thin skinned, and egotistical beyond the scope of the word. And he lies as easily as he breathes.

Did some voters disregard politics and finally feel they just couldn’t stand him anymore?

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

item.title: An optimistic October jobs report
item.description:
The U.S. labor market added 165,000 jobs in October, which was more than expected. An uptick in white-collar hiring was particularly surprising. Sure, unemployment remains stuck just above 4%, but more jobs is a step in the right direction. Plus: Declining foreign ownership of U.S. Treasurys contributes to rising yield rates, more friends are co-homebuying in this unaffordable housing market, and we recap the post-election economic headlines.


Every story has an economic angle. Want some in your inbox? Subscribe to our daily or weekly newsletter.


Marketplace is more than a radio show. Check out our original reporting and financial literacy content at marketplace.org — and consider making an investment in our future.

  • Latest jobs report shows a white-collar hiring turnaround
  • Foreign governments own fewer Treasurys these days. That's pushing interest rates up
  • Want to buy a house with friends? This Colorado group did it

item.title: Refineries are rethinking what they produce
item.description:
A new analysis from the federal Energy Information Administration shows that this year, oil refineries in the U.S. have been shifting some of their production capacity away from gasoline. They’re producing more “middle distillates,” which includes jet fuel and diesel. The global supply of those products has been tight. Later in the episode, we’ll continue to look at the success of populist political candidates in the U.S. and abroad.

item.title: Teaching financial advisors the depth behind tools and recipes
item.description:
When you cook, do you follow a recipe precisely or adapt it as you go? My wife uses the second approach. She will make something extraordinary, and when I ask if she wrote down what she did, she has no idea. She tasted, adjusted, and added a little of this or that. I am the opposite. Give me a recipe, and I’m fine; just don’t ask me to be creative.

That’s probably why, in my long-ago first sales job in real estate, I initially relied on the decision tree the manager gave me. “If the client says this, go here. If they object, go there.” I tried to memorize every branch. If a customer said something that wasn’t on any of them, I had nothing.

You have probably sat across from someone like that, maybe an insurance agent reading from a script or a financial advisor going through a standard questionnaire without looking up. You can feel the difference when someone is rigidly following a recipe rather than listening to you and responding to your needs and concerns.

The difference matters when someone is handling your financial life. Most advisor training works tool-first. You learn the exercise, practice it, and repeat it until you know the recipe and master the skill.

Breanna Blaney, founder of the Anya Institute and creator of the Integrative Wealth Advisor certification, uses a different approach to train financial advisors. Before her students learn any client-facing tools, they spend months doing their own inner work, examining their own relationship with money and their own blind spots. Only then do they learn the techniques. “I teach people how to cook,” she says, “not what the recipe is.”

When I introduce the emotional side of money to my financial planning students at Golden Gate University, the most common reaction is shock that it was never part of their formal education. “This is hard,” they say when I ask them to sit quietly with their own thoughts for a few minutes. If it is that hard for them, imagine how difficult it is for a planner without that practice to guide clients through their money issues.

Jacob Moreno, the founder of psychodrama, used the phrase “getting on the balcony” to describe rising above the action to observe what is actually happening rather than reacting. A financial advisor on the balcony asks better questions, notices what you are not saying, and does not flinch when the conversation moves past the numbers. Blaney’s description for this is, “I’m looking at you. I’m seeing you first.”

In practice, that means the advisor does not default to running you through the same sequence of questions, exercises, or rote processes they use with every client. They will not rush past the emotion to get to the spreadsheet. If you need to talk about why you cannot bring yourself to sell your late parents’ house before you can discuss the tax implications, an advisor who has done their own work will follow you there.

If you are looking for a financial advisor, here are some clues that someone knows how to cook rather than just how to follow a recipe:

  1. They ask about your life before they ask about your portfolio.

  2. They listen and clarify before they offer advice.

  3. They can sit with a difficult subject without changing it.

  4. They have examined their own relationship with money before trying to guide yours.

For a financial advisor, having a recipe book of skills and processes is essential. Just as important is knowing when and how to tweak those recipes to give clients the service and support they need.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

The information provided is for educational purposes only and should not be construed as investment advice. The views expressed are subject to change based on market or economic conditions. Past performance is not indicative of future results. Any reference to potential benefits is illustrative and may not apply to your individual circumstances. You should consult with your financial adviser before making any investment decisions. KFG, LLC is an SEC-registered Investment Adviser.

item.title: Tesla to end Cybertruck production as sales stall at ~10% of plan
item.description:
Tesla is ending Cybertruck production. CEO Elon Musk announced early Friday that the automaker will “wind down” the electric pickup at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, about three and a half years after the first deliveries.

Musk says it’s to make room for more Cybercab production. But Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck is short on buyers, and it sells at roughly a tenth of the 250,000 units a year Tesla built its line for.

item.title: Data centers lost in the midterms
item.description:
Voters have made their dissatisfaction quite clear with the tech status quo. And it sounds like the Democrats gearing up to take power in the House and Senate might actually do something about that.


Plus, Big Tech spent big on races in this election, but didn't get a whole lot of bang for their buck. But first, a tech issue that was actually on the ballot: data centers. More than 40 jurisdictions across 10 states voted to put them on ice. However, Harwood, North Dakota, gave them the green light. Paresh Dave, senior writer at Wired, joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino to explain more about all this on this week’s “Tech Bytes: Week in Review.”


More on this:


“America got the anti-data-center wave it voted for. Here come the economic consequences” from CNN


“After Midterm Rebuke, OpenAI Pledges to Give Data Center Towns More Say” from The New York Times


“AI & Tech Brief: Midterms turn the AI tide” from The Washington Post


“Democratic midterm wins set stage for tougher tech and AI scrutiny” from IAPP


“Elon Musk suffers major blow in US midterms” from Politico


“Ohio’s Senate Race Is a Rare Loss for Crypto Under Trump” from The New York Times


Check out our YouTube page to watch more episodes of “Tech Bytes.”

item.title: ChatGPT for Teens' safeguards don't work, risk assessment finds
item.description:
OpenAI's new teen-appropriate version of ChatGPT may not be living up to its promises, according to an independent evaluation. The new mode is supposed to have stronger guardrails for sensitive topics, automatic parental alerts and a study tool that won't just give kids the answers to their homework.


But the nonprofit Common Sense Media evaluated the tool and found it poses "unacceptable risks." Tom Siegel leads the Youth Safety Institute at Common Sense and tested about 4,000 prompts using fake teen accounts. He spoke with Meghan McCarty Carino about his findings.


More on this:


“ChatGPT for Teens Poses Unacceptable Risk to Kids, Common Sense Media Finds” from Common Sense Media

item.title: Farmers need help. Let’s see if a Dem-led congress can provide it
item.description:
Though grain and soybean prices have come up a bit in recent months, the American Farm Bureau thinks that farmers will continue to see tough times. Prices for their crops just aren’t  keeping up with input costs, principally fertilizer and diesel fuel. 

So far, the Trump administration’s policies haven’t been able to make much of a difference by way of financial relief, so the White House turned to making direct cash payments to farmers in order for many of them to stay afloat.

Much as I support federal financial aid in order to keep producers functioning – food security is priority number one – an efficiently structured relationship between farmers and policy-makers in Washington is what the ag industry needs.

The Trump administration has been helpless when it comes to framing policy that works for farmers, which makes cash bailouts a necessity and only extends official ineptitude.  

Last night’s overwhelming rejection of Trump and his policies was driven in large part by rural states that turned on the president’s party. Though South Dakota didn’t participate in the political overhaul, farmers in our state will be impacted by the changes in ag policies that should materialize in D.C. next year.  

The first order of business should be passing a Farm Bill. Agriculture is a high risk business, subjected to sometimes wild price fluctuations and the vagaries of weather. Farm bills provide safety nets that farmers and their lenders can depend on. 

Farmers also need an administration that knows something about how trade policy can affect rural livelihoods. Trump’s wild and irrational trade wars have permanently altered the soybean market, and not for the better as far as American producers are concerned.

Now that Democrats from rural areas are part of the political landscape in D.C. we should expect better when it comes to dealing with the headstrong Trump, who up to now had a Republican congress green-lighting policies that drove crop prices down and pushed input prices up.

Will the Democrats perform? I think they will, especially as much of their newfound political strength comes from the rural districts that terminated their Republican reps yesterday. 

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission. 

Photo: South Dakota farm, public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

The first order of business should be [passing a Farm Bill](https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/who-we-are/how-we-work/policy/supporting-the-farm-bill/). Agriculture is a high risk business, subjected to sometimes wild price fluctuations and the vagaries of weather. Farm bills provide safety nets that farmers and their lenders can depend on.
Farmers also need an administration that knows something about how trade policy can affect rural livelihoods. Trump’s wild and irrational trade wars have [permanently altered the soybean market](https://www.investopedia.com/soybean-exports-to-china-are-gone-and-may-never-fully-recover-11835118), and not for the better as far as [American producers](https://www.cato.org/blog/trumps-trade-wars-harm-farmers-taxpayers) are concerned.
Now that Democrats from rural areas are part of the political landscape in D.C. we should expect better when it comes to dealing with the headstrong Trump, who up to now had a Republican congress [green-lighting](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/26/donald-trump-policy-disaster-rural-america) policies that [drove crop prices down](https://www.cato.org/blog/trumps-trade-wars-harm-farmers-taxpayers) and [pushed input prices up](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/08/25/farmers-say-they-face-new-crisis-trumps-tariffs-iran-war-raise-costs/).
Will the Democrats perform? I think they will, especially as much of their newfound political strength comes from the rural districts that terminated their Republican reps yesterday.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Germany’s EV share hits record 37% as BEVs beat gas and diesel combined
item.description:
Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.

For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.

more…
item.source:markdown:

item.title: Song sung blue? No. Last night was the Hallelujah Chorus sung blue
item.description:
Last night’s rebuke of Donald Trump should be a long-needed slap in the GOP’s collective face. His party has needed to come out of its Trump-induced stupor for a long time. 

Trump caused this because he has taken the Republican Party on a path that has veered away from long-standing conservative principles, creating problems that led to a sweeping rejection of him and his loyalists.

If Trump had been true to Republican principles, this wouldn’t have happened.  

  • If Trump had followed traditional GOP practice and ideology, his tariff binge would not have occurred. Republicans have historically been champions of free trade. During the Reagan and Bush era, free trade initiatives, particularly the development of the World Trade Organization, were a top priority. Back in 2017, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds was writing about the benefits of trade agreements and their importance to South Dakota. Trump’s tariff agenda has been bad for South Dakota and the country in  general, particularly on the inflation front.

  • Trump’s rhetoric on immigration completely reversed the attitude that was prevalent during the Reagan-Bush era. Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric and policies have had a negative effect on the economy.

  • Trump’s energy policies, which lead to greater dependence on fossil fuels, have been a disaster. “Drill, baby, drill” is about the dumbest approach to energy management I can think of, and I think about it every time I have to shell out serious bucks for a tankful of gasoline.  George W. Bush was a strong supporter of renewable energy.  Why Trump won’t follow suit is a mystery. 

The common denominator for the way Trump has turned away from policies common to his recent Republican predecessors in the White House is inflation – and clearly, inflation is one of the main causes of the discontent that led to last night’s debacle. Trump has created an identity crisis for his party, and the public has just shown that it has had enough of it.

Hallelujah.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
Last night’s rebuke of Donald Trump should be a long-needed slap in the GOP’s collective face. His party has needed to come out of its Trump-induced stupor for a long time.
Trump caused this because he has taken the Republican Party on a path that has veered away from long-standing conservative principles, creating problems that led to a sweeping rejection of him and his loyalists.
If Trump had been true to Republican principles, this wouldn’t have happened.
- If Trump had followed [traditional GOP practice and ideology](https://abcnews.com/Business/past-republican-presidents-tariffs/story?id=116268942), his tariff binge would not have occurred. Republicans have historically been champions of free trade. During the Reagan and Bush era, free trade initiatives, particularly the development of the World Trade Organization, were a top priority. [Back in 2017](https://www.rounds.senate.gov/newsroom/weekly-column/trade-agreements-vital-to-south-dakotas-economy), South Dakota senator Mike Rounds was writing about the benefits of trade agreements and their importance to South Dakota. Trump’s tariff agenda has been [bad for South Dakota](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2025/05/27/south-dakota-governors-economic-advisers-bemoan-trumps-tariff-policy/) and the country in general, [particularly on the inflation front](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/tracking-economic-effects-tariffs).
- Trump’s [rhetoric on immigration](https://theconversation.com/republicans-once-championed-immigration-in-the-us-why-has-the-partys-rhetoric-and-public-opinion-changed-so-dramatically-239836) completely reversed the attitude that was prevalent during the Reagan-Bush era. Trump’s exclusionary rhetoric and policies have had a [negative effect](https://equitablegrowth.org/economic-research-shows-immigration-is-good-for-u-s-workers-the-economy-and-affordability/) on the economy.
- Trump’s [energy policies](https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/inflation-numbers-show-trump-administration-energy-policies-infecting-nations), which lead to greater dependence on fossil fuels, have been a disaster. [“Drill, baby, drill”](https://www.google.com/search?q=drill+baby+drill+trump&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=drill+baby+drill&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUqDAgBEAAYFBiHAhiABDIGCAAQRRg5MgwIARAAGBQYhwIYgAQyBwgCEAAYgAQyBwgDEAAYgAQyBwgEEAAYgAQyBwgFEAAYgAQyCggGEAAYgAQYtAcyBwgHEAAYgAQyBwgIEAAYgAQyBwgJEAAYgATSAQg3NjI1ajBqN6gCALACAA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) is about the dumbest approach to energy management I can think of, and I think about it every time I have to shell out serious bucks for a tankful of gasoline. [George W. Bush was a strong supporter](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-president-bush-signs-into-law-national-energy-plan) of renewable energy. Why Trump won’t follow suit is a mystery.
The common denominator for the way Trump has turned away from policies common to his recent Republican predecessors in the White House is [inflation](https://fortune.com/2025/08/16/trump-deportation-immigration-inflation-2026/) – and clearly, inflation is one of the main causes of the discontent that led to last night’s debacle. Trump has created an identity crisis for his party, and the public has just shown that it has had enough of it.
Hallelujah.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. item.title: Data centers were on the ballot. They lost.
item.description:
Voter frustration with the economy helped the Democrats win control of Congress. But data centers were also on the ballot yesterday, and they got a big thumbs down from voters. Voters were deciding on more than 40 data center measures. According to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot, voters passed 33 provisions to restrict data centers. Only one proposal to allow more data centers passed. Plus, the day after midterms, how should you navigate political conversations at work?

item.description:

A growing number of lawsuits accuse AI companies of harming users — alleging chatbots have encouraged self-harm, reinforced delusions, or failed to recognize signs of distress.


And yet at the same time, a growing number of users, particularly younger ones, say they're turning to AI for emotional support.


Dr. John Torous studies how technology interacts with mental health. He says in the case of AI, it's complicated.

item.source:markdown:
**_This story includes references to suicide, self-harm and mental health crises. If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call or text 988 to reach the_** **_[Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/)_** **_. Available 24/7._**
A growing number of [lawsuits](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-chatbots-serious-psychological-harms) accuse AI companies of harming users — alleging chatbots have encouraged self-harm, reinforced delusions, or failed to recognize signs of distress.
And yet at the same time, a growing number of users, particularly younger ones, [say they're turning to AI for emotional support.](https://www.rand.org/news/press/2026/06/nearly-1-in-5-us-adolescents-and-young-adults-use-ai.html)
Dr. John Torous studies how technology interacts with mental health. He says in the case of AI, it's complicated.
_More on this:_
[Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/30/nx-s1-6022278/ai-artificial-intelligence-teens-jed-common-sense-media) — from NPR

item.title: When it comes to the job market, love the one you're with
item.description:
The September Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey from the BLS is out, and things in this labor market are mostly unchanged, although quits were up a bit. Still, economists are clear: Now is not the time to leave your job without another one lined up. Also in this episode: That stiff labor market may be hampering productivity, warehousing costs are up as retailers scramble for the holidays, and pro baseball faces a lockout in 2027.

  • Quits ticked up in September, but economists say it’s still a terrible time to leave your job
  • Sometimes leaving the workforce turns into a labor of love
  • Why warehouse space is getting harder and more expensive to come by
  • Companies invest big in pet food research

item.title: Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe
item.description:
Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

item.title: Why so many men are opting out of the workforce
item.description:
It’s a big week for labor market data, including data on wages, unemployment, and job turnover. But before the employment floodgates open, it’s worth looking at a group of workers who have stepped back from the labor force: Men ages 25 to 54 — who were almost all working half a century ago — are participating significantly less today. What gives? Also: a look at how the U.S. trade balance is holding up.

item.title: Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay
item.description:
Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

more…
item.source:markdown:
![](https://electrek.co/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/Tesla-Megapack-3-Megablock.webp?w=1600)
Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, [published in the Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/02/2026-22301/foreign-trade-zone-ftz-84-authorization-of-production-activity-tesla-inc-battery-storage-products) on Monday, runs for 14 months.
It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.
[more…](https://electrek.co/2026/11/03/tesla-megapack-texas-foreign-trade-zone-china-tariffs/#more-490686)

item.title: What are tokenized stocks?
item.description:
Back in September, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission cleared the way for the trading of tokenized stocks. The so-called “Innovation Exemption” temporarily lifts some regulations to allow for the issuance of digital tokens, which represent shares in a corporation or organization. In other words, it’s another way for investors to trade. This morning, we explain it all. But first, Marriott’s earnings beat expectations, even as some customers tighten their belts.

item.title: How Dick Nixon tried to kill South Dakota Senator Karl Mundt
item.description:
Author’s note: The difference between a memoir and an autobiography is that a memoir tells the story as best the author can remember it.  An autobiography has to be fact-checked.  This falls into the category of mini-memoir.  

As a young speech and social studies instructor at Eastern State Normal School in the 1930s in Madison, South Dakota, once upon a time a teacher college that is now known as Dakota State University, Karl Mundt developed a name for two reasons. He founded the National Forensics League, a speech and debate organization for high school students nationwide. He traveled around eastern South Dakota demonstrating his skill as a public speaker.  Soon the idea arose that it might be good if someday he might run for Congress. Since the Board of Regents could not abide political campaigning by its employees, Mundt was summoned to the Dean’s office.

You are an outstanding speech instructor, the Dean supposedly told him, and I do not want to lose you, but as a possible political candidate you cannot have a contract to teach here. “I do not need a contract,” Mundt replied. “I shall be happy to continue teaching, but if after two weeks there is no pay envelope in my mailbox, my enthusiasm for teaching will wane considerably.”

In 1938 he won a seat in Congress, then later the Senate. He was on the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he taught young California Congressman Richard Nixon how to hunt Commies. In 1954 Mundt chaired the Army-McCarthy hearings.  He rose to become second-ranking Republican on the Appropriations Committee and delivered a fair amount of pork to South Dakota.  

In 1969 he suffered a major stroke. His wife Mary, whom he met and married at University, believed he would recover and rebuffed efforts to have Karl step aside. As 1970 dawned it became clear that a Democrat might defeat Governor Frank Farrar and win the Governorship, and with it the ability to appoint a replacement to Mundt if he should die in office. Republican leaders wanted him to resign so Republican Farrar could appoint a replacement before the Democrats took the Governor’s Mansion. 

First a hometown delegation of Republicans appeared at the door to Mundt’s home on Capitol Hill. Mary fussed in the kitchen and made coffee for them. We must protect this seat for the GOP, they argued.  Karl deserves to enjoy well-earned retirement. Mary scolded them for being disloyal.  

Next a delegation of statewide Republican leaders knocked on the door.  A gracious welcome, but same thing. Shame on you, she said. 

South Dakota’s Republican Governor Frank Farrar also tried, but that had no chance. Farrar had been floating the idea of running against Karl in the 1972 Republican primary. Mary adamantly opposed Karl’s resigning if it meant Farrar might appoint himself to the Senate seat.  

Not long after that a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt residence.  Out came the President of the United States, Richard M. Nixon. He walked to the door and knocked. Mary welcomed him in. “Oh, Mr. President, Karl will be so happy to see you.” Mundt was sitting on a couch and may have been cognizant but, because of his stroke, was unable to string words together — a horrible loss for such a powerful orator. 

While Mary was in the kitchen fussing to make coffee, the Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces turned to the young Naval orderly who was helping care for the Senator. Nixon pointed to cigar boxes on the top shelf of a bookcase. “What are those?” he asked. 

“We have to constantly hide cigars from the Senator,” was the reply. “The doctor says if he smokes another he will have a big stroke and die."

Thereafter, once a week a black limousine pulled up to the Mundt home and a representative of the White House personally handed the Senator a box of cigars from President Nixon.

Jody Severson is a retired political and marketing consultant whose first campaign was "Clean for Gene" McCarthy in 1968.  He was a consultant in scores of campaigns at the statewide, local, and national levels from the north woods of Minnesota to the bayous of Louisiana. A native of Madison, SD, he has lived in Rapid City since the 1980s. 

Photo: Then U.S. Representative Karl Mundt, 1940, public domain, wikimedia commons

item.title: Why raise money in euros?

item.title: Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls
item.description:
Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

item.title: My wish list if there is a blue wave in tomorrow’s election
item.description:
If the Democrats take Congress tomorrow, fixing Trump’s mess should be the first item on the legislative agenda.

From an ag-oriented South Dakotan’s perspective, I want to see Congress undo the president’s tariffs.  It has the power to do so. They’ve been such a drag on our country’s farm economy that getting rid of them will loosen up long-standing supply chain disruptions and get some liquidity back into the world’s distribution networks.

Congress should use all the tools at its disposal to get Trump to end his useless war in Iran. Its inflationary impact and waste of lives and money need to cease.

Problems of affordability have to be addressed, and they will be if tariffs are rescinded and the Iran war comes to a close. More broadly, Congress can address the affordability crisis through legislative actions aimed at housing supply, tax policy, and health care costs.

Given the way climate change is accelerating, we need more in in the way of green energy incentives and fossil fuel regulation.

Immigration policy should be focused on getting undocumented but otherwise law-abiding immigrants on the pathways to legalization. This was Ronald Reagan’s approach, and it worked. Trump’s policy of rounding them up and deporting them wholesale amounts to a deplorable lack of humanity. If you have a Judeo-Christian bent, read Leviticus 19:33-34. If you’re focused on the practical, economic consequences of Trump’s heavy-handed policy, consider that it’s causing a labor shortage in this country.

The list is long and complex, but a resounding political mandate tomorrow will at least make it approachable.

Let’s get out there and vote.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

Its [inflationary impact](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/13/economy/iran-war-oil-gas-prices-inflation) and waste of lives and money need to cease.
_Problems of affordability_ have to be addressed, and they will be if tariffs are rescinded and the Iran war comes to a close. More broadly, [Congress can address](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13189) the affordability crisis through legislative actions aimed at housing supply, tax policy, and health care costs.
_Given the way climate change is_ [_accelerating_](https://e360.yale.edu/digest/warming-gaining-pace), we need more in in the way of green energy incentives and fossil fuel regulation.
_Immigration policy_ should be focused on getting undocumented but otherwise law-abiding immigrants on the pathways to legalization. This was [Ronald Reagan’s approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_Reform_and_Control_Act_of_1986), and it worked. [Trump’s policy](https://www.cfr.org/articles/ice-and-deportations-how-trump-reshaping-immigration-enforcement) of rounding them up and deporting them wholesale amounts to a deplorable lack of humanity. If you have a Judeo-Christian bent, read [Leviticus 19:33-34](https://www.bible.com/bible/111/LEV.19.33-34.NIV). If you’re focused on the practical, economic consequences of Trump’s heavy-handed policy, consider that it’s [causing a labor shortage](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jul/29/trump-immigration-crackdown-labor-shortages-slowdowns) in this country.
The list is long and complex, but a resounding political mandate tomorrow will at least make it approachable.
Let’s get out there and vote.

item.title: What it means when AI helps solve complex math problems
item.description:
In September, OpenAI said that its models had solved one of math's famous Millennium Prize problems. Then, the lab dropped more than 700 papers tackling another 400 complex problems with more breakthroughs to come.


These developments have caused something of an existential crisis in the math world. But Alex Kontorovich, a professor of math at Rutgers University, says they're a gift.

item.description:
Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

item.title: We have a winner in the Iran war, and the winner is …
item.description:
… the oil industry and its shareholders. Glancing across yesterday’s earning reports on the financial sites, the first headline I encountered in The Wall Street Journal announced “American Oil Giants See Profits Soar as Wars Crimp Energy Supplies.” The sub-head? “ExxonMobil and Chevron post blockbuster earnings for third quarter as world turns to U.S. refineries for fuel.” 

ExxonMobil’s profits doubled compared to the same period last year. Chevron’s were up 185%. Meantime, we consumers are gagging at our local gas pumps, paying an average of $4.12/gallon, about a buck over what we were paying a year ago.

This is what Donald Trump has wrought. 

Though he has since claimed that he was misinterpreted, Trump at the onset of the war said that it would be over in a matter of weeks. Since then the timeline has shifted. The last I heard, he said the war will end “soon,” a comfortably meaningless word when it comes to specificty. That and his claims of being misunderstood only amplify his incoherence on the subject.

That Trump recently said “we’re in the golden age of America … our nation is doing better now than ever before” only amplifies his detachment from reality.

Meanwhile, as the back and forth on what-Trump-said vs. what-Trump-meant goes on, the practical effect of Trump’s invasion of Iran has been to make oil producers much, much richer and helpless oil consumers all the poorer.

As to the president trying to do something about high fuel costs, Trump has come up way short. His feeble efforts to ease diesel fuel prices by engineering a deal that would let Russia increase diesel fuel exports were a fantasy (Foreign Policy calls the deal a “hail Mary”) from the get-go. Not only have diesel prices not gone down, they’ve actually risen by 7 cents/gallon since the deal was announced.

On the gasoline front, Trump’s only utterances about potentially lower prices are that gas will get cheaper once the Iran war ends. That stands to reason, but the price-dropping process will be slow-going once the Strait of Hormuz opens."If and when that happens, it will be a very long, multi-month to multi-year process for things to fully normalize,"  says a GasBuddy petroleum expert quoted on CBS.

The economically painful results of Trump’s hapless venture into the Persian Gulf will linger for a long time. The Center for Strategic and International Studies sees localized conflicts, many of them stirred up during Trump’s incursion into the area, as a “postwar threat to Gulf energy infrastructure.”

Unclear as Trump’s objectives in this war have been, his options seem even more muddled, which is a natural follow-up to the discordant statements and erratic strategies that got us into this mess in the first place.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and comm,entary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: The link between immigration raids and the housing shortage
item.description:
Homebuilders constructed 19,000 fewer homes in 2024 because of the lack of skilled labor, according to a construction industry estimate from last year. A big factor in the labor shortage is the federal government's immigration crackdown, which has led to the arrest of many construction workers, often at job sites. This morning, we hear from some families and businesses impacted. Also: weighing jobs and tax revenue versus pollution concerns near proposed data centers.
